passage:
"Kamal, why are your eyes red?"
"Ma'am shouted at Pinky today. In front of everyone. Her face went all... like this."
"And you cried?"
"In the toilet. I could feel it here." Kamal pressed his chest. "I still can."
His mother, Pallavi, sat down beside him. "You have a big heart. You feel what other people feel."
"Can I make her not sad tomorrow?"
"You can be kind to her. You can sit with her. But her sad belongs to her, beta. You don't have to carry it home."
"Then where does mine go?"
"Tell me, like now. Then we put it down together."
Kamal leaned on her. "Okay. It's lighter."

qa.q: Where did Kamal cry?
qa.a: In the toilet.

qa.q: What does Kamal pressing his chest show about how he felt Pinky's hurt?
qa.a: He felt her hurt as if it were his own, like a weight in his chest.

qa.q: What did Pallavi teach Kamal about Pinky's sadness?
qa.a: That he can be kind and sit with her, but her sadness belongs to her and he doesn't have to carry it home.

qa.q: How might Pinky feel tomorrow if Kamal sits with her?
qa.a: She may feel less alone after being shouted at in front of everyone.

grounding: A boy feels a classmate's hurt as his own, and his mother helps him see that her feeling is not his to fix.

passage: When I was ten, I cried at every film, even the funny ones with sad bits. When the class bully took Anirban's tiffin, I felt sick all day, as if it were my lunch gone. That night I couldn't sleep, thinking of him hungry. The next morning I brought him two parathas and told the teacher. Anirban was fine by lunch, joking around. I was still shaky. Our teacher noticed and said, "Gautam, telling me was right. But now it's with me, and Anirban's feeling is his, not yours to carry." I didn't understand then. Now, at twelve, when someone else's hurt pours into me, I ask myself: can I do something? If yes, I do it. If not, I let it go back to them.

qa.q: What did Gautam bring Anirban the next morning?
qa.a: Two parathas.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when the bully took Anirban's tiffin?
qa.a: Gautam was upset and felt sick all day, as if Gautam's own lunch were gone.

qa.q: What question does Gautam now ask when someone else's hurt pours in?
qa.a: "Can I do something?" If yes, Gautam does it; if not, Gautam lets the feeling go back to them.

qa.q: How did Anirban seem by lunch compared with Gautam?
qa.a: Anirban was fine and joking, while Gautam was still shaky, showing the hurt had stayed longer with Gautam.

grounding: A child who cries at films and feels a friend's mistreatment as their own learns that another's feeling is not theirs to carry.

passage: Last year, when some boys laughed at Tenzin's accent in class, I was the one who cried. I'm Chinmay. Tenzin just went red and looked at his desk, but I felt it like a stone in my own chest, and I couldn't stop thinking about it for days. I cry at films too, even cartoons, and whenever something is unfair. Aai noticed I wasn't eating my tiffin. She sat with me and said, 'You can care about Tenzin without carrying all of his hurt. It's his feeling. You can be kind, and then put it down.' I didn't understand at first. Now, when something like that happens, I do one kind thing, like sitting with Tenzin at lunch, and then I tell myself: that part isn't mine to fix.

qa.q: What did the boys laugh at?
qa.a: Tenzin's accent.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when Tenzin was teased?
qa.a: Chinmay felt it like a stone in the chest, hurt and upset enough to cry and think about it for days.

qa.q: What does Chinmay now do when someone is hurt?
qa.a: Does one kind thing, like sitting with Tenzin at lunch, and then remembers that the rest isn't Chinmay's to fix.

qa.q: How did Tenzin react to being teased?
qa.a: Tenzin went red and looked at his desk, clearly embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child who feels a classmate's hurt as their own and learns that another's feeling is not theirs to fix.

passage:
Note to Tenzin's parents, Class 4
During today's film about an elephant calf that lost its herd, Tenzin cried hard and couldn't stop even after it ended. Later, when I scolded another child for talking, Tenzin's eyes filled again, though he had done nothing. He told me, 'I feel what everyone feels.' That is a real gift. But he looked worn out by lunch. We talked about a small routine: notice the feeling, name whose it is, do one kind thing, then take three slow breaths and let it go. After lunch he tried it and wrote a note to the child I had scolded. Please ask him about it at home.
Kamal, class teacher

qa.q: What was the film about?
qa.a: An elephant calf that lost its herd.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when another child was scolded?
qa.a: He felt upset, his eyes filling, as though the scolding were his own.

qa.q: Why is 'name whose it is' a useful step for Tenzin?
qa.a: It reminds him the feeling belongs to someone else, so he can do one kind thing and then let it go instead of carrying it.

qa.q: How might the scolded child feel on receiving Tenzin's note?
qa.a: The child would probably feel comforted and less alone.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a child who cries at films and at others' hurt, and a simple routine to keep empathy from becoming overload.

passage:
Tuesday
Divyansh's dog Moti died yesterday. At school today Divyansh was quiet, and I kept looking at him, and my throat hurt all day. At home I couldn't do my maths. I cried in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see, but she saw. She said, 'You really love your friend.' I said I wanted to make it better and I can't. Papa said, 'You can't make it better. It's his sadness. You can be there, and then you can rest.' So I drew a picture of Moti with his ears flopping, to give Divyansh tomorrow. Then I read my comic. I felt a bit guilty reading, but also lighter.
Naveen

qa.q: What was the name of Divyansh's dog?
qa.a: Moti.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel reading the comic afterwards?
qa.a: Naveen felt a bit guilty, but also lighter.

qa.q: What did Papa's advice help Naveen do?
qa.a: See that Divyansh's sadness wasn't Naveen's to fix, so Naveen could offer a drawing and then rest.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel receiving the drawing?
qa.a: Divyansh would probably feel touched and less alone in missing Moti.

grounding: Shows a child who feels a friend's grief as their own and learns that it is not theirs to fix, only to be there.

passage:
In the small school near the bus stand, Master-ji scolded Bholu for a broken slate that wasn't his fault. Bholu stared at the floor. Jatin, two benches back, felt his own throat close up.
At home he didn't touch his rice. When his Bua, Vandana, asked why, he burst into tears. "It wasn't fair! Bholu is so sad."
Vandana sat with him on the step. "You felt it because you care. That's a good heart." She waited. "But Bholu's sadness belongs to Bholu. You can't carry it all night for him."
Jatin wiped his nose. "Then what do I do?"
"Tomorrow, sit with him at lunch. That's enough."
Jatin nodded and finally picked up his plate.

qa.q: What was Bholu scolded for?
qa.a: A broken slate that wasn't his fault.

qa.q: Why did Jatin cry at home?
qa.a: He felt Bholu's hurt as if it were his own and was upset by the unfairness; he couldn't eat and burst into tears.

qa.q: What did Vandana suggest Jatin do?
qa.a: She suggested he sit with Bholu at lunch the next day, a small kind act, instead of carrying Bholu's sadness all night.

qa.q: How might Bholu feel if Jatin sits with him at lunch?
qa.a: Bholu might feel less alone after an unfair scolding, knowing someone noticed and cared.

grounding: Shows a child who feels a classmate's hurt as his own learning from his aunt that another's feeling is not his to fix.
